text: FunSearch Weibull heuristic: score = (bins - max(bins))**2 / item + bins**2 / item**2 + bins**2 / item**3; negate the score for bins with bins > item; then score[1:] -= score[:-1], the difference with the preceding bin's score, which makes bin order matter.

Fill-probability lookahead from the item stream seen so far: keep a running histogram h of item sizes; priority = -r + lam * P(a future item has size in [r-1, r]) where r = bins - item and P = h / sum(h); lam = 20. Bins whose gap a common item size can close are preferred.

NON-MONOTONE   STEP   TABLE   ON   THE   RESIDUAL   R   =   BINS   -   ITEM,   AS   IN   THE   FUNSEARCH   OR3   HEURISTIC:   SCORE   4   FOR   R   <=   2,   3   FOR   R   <=   3,   2   FOR   R   <=   5,   1   FOR   R   <=   7,   0.9   FOR   R   <=   9,   THEN   0.95,   0.97,   0.98,   0.99   FOR   LARGER   R.   MID-SIZED   GAPS   (8-9)   SCORE   BELOW   LARGE   ONES,   SO   THE   HEURISTIC   AVOIDS   LEAVING   GAPS   FEW   ITEMS   CAN   FILL.

CMA-ES over 8 coefficients of a linear score on features [r, r^2, item, item*r, 1/(r+1), fill probability (#26), bin age, fragment flag], trained on OR3 instances 0-9 and tested on instances 10-19 and on Weibull.
Penalise leftover gaps quadratically: priority = -(bins - item)**2, so a large residual capacity is punished much more than a small residual.
Harmonic-k packing with k = 6: put each item into a size class by the interval (C/(i+1), C/i] and pack a class only into bins reserved for that class, using best fit inside the class.
Replace the running histogram in the fill-probability score with a Gaussian kernel density estimate of item sizes (bandwidth 2) to get a smoother fill probability.
Test the Weibull polynomial heuristic with its differencing step score[1:] -= score[:-1] removed, to see whether the neighbour difference is needed.
Sample the bin from a softmax over best-fit priorities, with probability proportional to exp(-r / T) at temperature T = 0.5, instead of taking the argmax.
Tune the 8-feature linear score with CMA-ES using both OR3 and Weibull in the objective: minimise the max of each dataset's excess divided by its gate threshold.
Cap the number of partially filled bins at K = 20: any bin beyond the 20 most recently opened is treated as closed and excluded from placement.
Fragment penalty: subtract M = 100 from a bin's priority whenever the residual it would leave is positive but smaller than the smallest item size seen so far.
Rank each container by the negated square of the slack that would remain once the parcel is inserted, so that big leftover headroom is punished disproportionately.

Segregate arrivals into six size bands whose edges are reciprocals of integers; each band owns dedicated containers, parcels never cross bands, and inside a band a parcel goes to the tightest container.
Learn the empirical law of parcel sizes online and favour the container whose remaining headroom is most likely to be closed off by some upcoming parcel, traded off against tightness.

Quadratic and cubic ratios of container headroom to parcel size, sign-flipped when the container has room to spare, after which every container's value is replaced by its excess over its predecessor's value (a first-order difference along container order).

A hand-built lookup of preference against leftover headroom that is not monotone: very tight leftovers score highest, middling leftovers of eight or nine units score lowest, and wide leftovers sit in between.

Covariance-adapting evolution strategy to fit the weights of a hand-crafted linear scorer over eight descriptors of each container, fitted on half of the capacity-150 benchmark and checked on the other half.
Hold back a look-ahead window of five arrivals and insert them largest-first.
Pick the scoring rule according to which benchmark is running, recognised from the container size.
Make it costlier to start a fresh container: every untouched container gets a flat deduction so that it is chosen only when no used one can take the parcel.
Protect roomy containers: forbid little parcels from entering a container that still has half or more of its room free, except as a last resort, so that big parcels later find space.
Weibull-shaped penalty on leftover capacity: priority = -r * (1 + (r / 20)**1.5), which punishes medium gaps super-linearly while keeping tight fits cheap.
Prefer the bin the item fills exactly; failing that, the bin left with the smallest gap; open an empty bin only when no used bin can take the item.

Make #27's kernel density fill probability fast: keep the KDE on a fixed grid over the integer sizes, updated incrementally by adding one kernel per arriving item, so scoring a bin is a table lookup rather than a pass over all past items; this targets the G-TIME failure (212 s).
Distil #47's MLP priority into a 32-entry lookup table over (residual bucket, item bucket) after training, so each evaluation is a table read; aimed at the 94 s runtime that stopped it.

The OR3 step table with its break points expressed in units of the running median item size instead of absolute units or capacity fractions, so the table adapts to Weibull's size distribution; aimed at the Weibull regression that stopped every table attempt.
#16's Weibull polynomial plus a fragment penalty that fires only when the residual after placement is below the smallest seen item, aimed at #16's OR3 loss, which comes from unusable small gaps.
#65's two-item fill probability computed with an FFT convolution of the histogram, refreshed every 500 items instead of per item, to bring the 71 s runtime under 60 s.
#66's CMA-ES linear scorer with the #11 step-table score added as a tenth feature, so the model can express the non-monotone gap preference that helps OR3; #66 missed G-OR by 0.04.
#36 (fragment penalty plus OR3 step table), but large items use #16's polynomial instead of the table, since #36's Weibull loss comes from large items the table misranks.
#74's closed-gap-fraction table with Bayesian shrinkage of each bucket toward the global closure rate, since sparse buckets on Weibull 5k gave noisy scores that cost G-WB.
#27's KDE fill probability with an Epanechnikov kernel of bandwidth 3 instead of a Gaussian kernel.
#16's polynomial with the first term using the mean bin residual instead of the max: (bins - mean(bins))**2 / item.
Harmonic-k with k = 8 classes instead of 6.
#47's MLP priority with three hidden layers of 8 units, trained with CMA-ES instead of OpenAI-ES.
The OR3 step table with one extra step: residual r <= 1 scores 5.
Softmax bin sampling with the temperature decaying from 2 to 0.1 over the stream.

Retry #28's two-sided fill probability with its crash fixed: the ZeroDivisionError came from p = h.get(r, 0) / total while total == 0 on each instance's first item. Initialise h with add-one (Laplace) counts over sizes 1..C so total > 0, and measure the unchanged mechanism.

#34's percentile fragment threshold was never exercised: its mask used r = item - bins (sign flipped), so (r > 0) & (r < q10) was always False. Recompute r = bins - item in the mask and measure the mechanism as designed.
#45's extra features 1/r and item/r were infinite at exact fits (r = 0), collapsing CMA-ES from generation 1. Use 1/(r + 0.5) and item/(r + 0.5) and rerun #45 as designed.

#75's per-instance reset cleared the count table on every priority() call because the module-level dict was cleared at function entry. Move the reset to instance start (detect a fresh bins array whose entries all equal capacity) and measure #75's adaptive table.
Re-run #28's two-sided fill probability; the crash was probably an implementation slip, so a careful reimplementation should work.
Try #45 again with cleaner code; the collapse looked like a numerical glitch.
Fix Harmonic-4's off-by-one class boundary (use floor(C / item) - 1 so size-75 items land in class 2) and measure Harmonic-4.

Differencing along time rather than along bin index: record for each bin the step at which it last received an item, and add to -r a bonus for bins untouched the longest, so stale bins are finished before their gaps drift out of reach.

Sum-of-Squares bin selection: choose the bin that minimises, after placement, the sum over gap sizes g of N(g)^2, where N(g) is the number of open bins with residual g; unlike squaring the residual, this squares the COUNTS of each gap size across bins.

Monte Carlo rollout from the running size histogram: for each candidate bin, sample 30 future items, pack them by best fit, and choose the bin whose rollouts open the fewest bins; the histogram is used to simulate, not to score gap closure.

Dual prices from the prefix: every 1,000 items solve the LP relaxation of the offline problem on the item-size histogram seen so far, and score a bin by the dual value of the sizes that could fill its residual; the L1 bound is replaced by LP duals as the guide.

Vectorise the step table itself: evaluate #11's table with np.searchsorted over its break points instead of the per-bin Python function s(bin, item), leaving every score unchanged but removing the Python loop.
Worst fit only for the first 5% of the stream, then best fit for the rest: spread the earliest items so that the opening bins cover a range of gap sizes before switching to tight packing.

Differencing of the item stream: use item - previous_item to predict whether the next item will be large, and if a rise is likely leave the current item out of the bins whose residual a large item needs.
Penalise bins by the variance of the item sizes already inside them, preferring bins whose contents are homogeneous in size, with -r as a tie-break.
Locality: place the current item into the bin the previous item went to whenever it fits there, otherwise best fit, exploiting runs of similar sizes in the stream.
Prefer bins holding fewer items: priority = -r - kappa * (number of items already in the bin), so bins filled by a few large items are completed before bins full of small items.

Learning-augmented profile packing: predict item-size frequencies from the prefix, build an offline profile of bin types from those frequencies, and route each arrival into a slot of the profile, opening a new profile copy when all slots of its type are taken.

Dynamic programming over an aggregated state: bucket open bins into 10 gap classes, keep the vector of class counts, and choose the placement that minimises a value function over that vector fitted by fitted value iteration on simulated streams.

A UCB1 bandit per item-size bucket chooses among best fit, the OR3 table and the Weibull polynomial for each arrival, rewarded every 100 items by the change in waste relative to the running lower bound.
Genetic programming over expression trees built from r, item, bin age and gap-count features, with trees bred for both datasets and simplified symbolically before scoring.

Profile packing: every 1,000 items, solve the prefix offline with first-fit decreasing, take the resulting bin types (multisets of item sizes) and their proportions as a template, and steer online placements toward completing template bin types, falling back to best fit when no template slot fits.

Pack online toward a template: periodically compute an offline first-fit-decreasing packing of the items seen so far, read off the recurring bin compositions and their frequencies, and route each new item into an open slot of the most needed composition.

Pick the container that keeps the multiset of leftover sizes flattest: after a tentative insertion, add up the squared number of containers sharing each leftover size, and choose the insertion with the smallest total.

Simulation-based choice: try each feasible container, play forward a few dozen sampled arrivals from the observed size law with tightest-fit packing, and keep the choice whose simulations start the fewest fresh containers.
Sum of squared residuals as a tie-break inside best fit: among bins within 1 unit of the tightest fit, prefer the one whose placement minimises the sum of squared residuals over all open bins.

Template from the offline LOWER BOUND, not a packing: use the L1 bound of the prefix to set a target fill level per bin and penalise bins whose fill after placement would exceed the running average target by more than one item size.
